analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties, disclosures, and court tools against employers who don't pay earned wages.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 25 Senate cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cracked down on wage theft — employers not paying the minimum wage, overtime, or final paychecks, which the bill's own findings estimate costs workers more than $15 billion a year. It would have required employers to give workers written pay terms, itemized paystubs, and final pay within 14 days of leaving a job, while doubling the window to sue for stolen wages and raising penalties, including mandatory referral for criminal prosecution of repeat offenders. It also would have barred employers from forcing workers into arbitration over wage claims and set up a $50 million-a-year grant program for community groups that help workers recover unpaid wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers who are shorted on pay. The bill's findings note women, immigrants, and Black workers are disproportionately hit by minimum wage violations, and a survey cited in the bill found 68 percent of low-wage workers in three major cities had experienced some form of wage theft in a single week. Workers who leave a job would get final pay within 14 days; workers who sue could recover double or triple damages plus interest over a four-year window (five for willful violations); and workers in noncompliant industries would get help from community organizations funded by new Labor Department grants.

how_it_helps.text: Employers would have to tell new hires their pay rate and overtime status in writing, and provide every pay period an itemized paystub showing hours worked, rates of pay, overtime, and deductions.
Workers would be owed their final pay within 14 days of leaving a job, and an employer who delays would owe the worker their regular rate for each day late, up to 30 days.

Workers who win wage claims could recover two to three times the unpaid wages plus interest, and the time limit for suing would double from two years to four (five for willful violations), with the clock paused while the Labor Department investigates.

Civil fines would rise to as much as $10,000 per affected employee for repeat or willful violations, and the Labor Department would be required to refer willful wage theft, falsified wage records, or retaliation against workers to the Justice Department for criminal prosecution.

Employers could no longer force workers to sign away their right to go to court over wages as a condition of employment, and workers would have the right to copies of their own wage records within 21 days of asking, with incomplete records counting in the worker's favor.

A $50 million-a-year grant program would fund nonprofits, unions, legal aid groups, and universities to educate workers about their rights, help them file claims, and partner with Wage and Hour Division investigators.

Where a contract or union agreement promises a wage above the federal minimum, the employer would have to actually pay that promised rate — closing a gap where workers could otherwise only recover the minimum wage.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who don't pay owed wages, who would face higher fines, double or triple damages, a longer window for lawsuits, possible criminal referral, and new paystub and recordkeeping duties. Compliant employers would bear modest new administrative costs for disclosures, paystubs, and record access, and taxpayers would fund the $50 million-a-year grant program through fiscal 2023.

drawbacks.text: The paperwork burden is real: every covered employer would need to issue detailed written pay terms within 15 days of hire, itemized paystubs meeting a long statutory list of contents, and copies of up to five years of wage records within 21 days of a worker's request — costs that fall hardest on small businesses with thin payroll systems.

Litigation exposure rises sharply: damages double or triple, the filing window doubles, the clock pauses during investigations, and if an employer's records are incomplete, a worker's own account of unpaid hours becomes a presumption the employer can only rebut with clear and convincing evidence — which could push more recordkeeping mistakes into costly settlements.

The bill would void pre-dispute arbitration agreements for wage claims, eliminating a faster, lower-cost dispute channel that many employers and some employees use, in favor of court and collective actions.
Mandatory criminal referral for willful wage violations and $50 million a year in new grant spending add to federal prosecutorial workload and federal outlays.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and concrete: the bill's own findings cite more than $15 billion a year in unpaid wages and DOL studies showing wage theft pushing tens of thousands of families into or deeper into poverty, against which the costs — payroll system upgrades, more lawsuits, and $50 million a year in grants — are modest and largely aimed at employers who are violating the law. The heavier litigation tools and record-based presumptions carry some risk of costly disputes over honest mistakes, and small employers face real compliance work, but the design targets penalties at repeat and willful violators rather than at compliant businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee in July 2019, and that committee never held a hearing or vote on it, so it simply expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on July 11, 2019, with 25 original cosponsors — 24 Democrats and the chamber's Independent — and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never reported the bill, and the full Senate never considered it for the rest of the 116th Congress.
The bill died on January 3, 2021, when the 116th Congress ended and unpassed bills lapse; nothing in its record shows a hearing, markup, floor vote, or a companion moving in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who short workers on pay are better off: they continue to face only the existing, light penalties and short two-year filing window, with no new paystub, disclosure, or record-access duties and no mandatory criminal referrals.

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 25 original cosponsors.

for.name: 25 Senate cosponsors (24 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; no Republican joined.

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee for its entire life.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor in the roughly 18 months after its introduction.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of them cosponsored the bill, leaving it with support only from Democrats and the chamber's Independent.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent, no Republican signed on, and the bill died in a Republican-chaired committee without ever reaching the floor.

industries.industry: Low-wage service employers (restaurants, retail, janitorial, agriculture, home care)
industries.note: These industries account for the bulk of wage and hour violations — the bill's findings note compliance below 50 percent in certain industries — so higher fines (up to $10,000 per affected employee for repeat violations), triple damages, a four- to five-year filing window, and possible criminal referral land mostly on them. Their interest in keeping current enforcement light runs directly against the workers they underpay.

industries.industry: Employers using forced arbitration and staffing/subcontracting arrangements
industries.note: The bill voids pre-dispute arbitration clauses for wage claims and requires the contract wage rate, including in collective bargaining agreements, to actually be paid — removing tools these employers use to keep wage disputes out of court and to shift down promised pay.

industries.industry: Nonprofit legal aid, worker centers, unions, and universities
industries.note: A new $50 million-a-year grant program would fund exactly these groups to educate workers, help file claims, and work alongside Wage and Hour Division investigators, creating a sustained funding stream for worker-side enforcement.

industries.industry: Employment law plaintiffs' bar and payroll compliance providers
industries.note: Doubled filing windows, triple damages, and mandatory paystubs would expand demand for wage-and-hour litigation and payroll compliance services; the gains ride on the same enforcement the bill directs at underpaying employers.
